newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan watchdog declines comment on Nomura report.
newsitem.headline: Japan watchdog declines comment on Nomura report.

text.p: Japan's securities watchdog on Wednesday declined comment on a newspaper report that it had decided to seek criminal action against Nomura Securities Co Ltd and two former executives involved in suspected illegal deals.
"We are not making any comments," the official with the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC) said.
The Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper reported on Wednesday that the SESC had concluded that Nomura itself made money through the dealings of the two former executives.

Nomura said last week that two of its directors had made deals that appeared to be "discretionary" transactions, meaning they were done without the client's knowledge, and moved profits raised from Nomura's own funds into a corporate client's account, practices banned under Japan's securities law. Media reports have linked the corporate client with a former "sokaiya" racketeer.
Government sources said on Wednesday that the SESC was still conducting a fact-finding investigation and that was unlikely to be concluded quickly.

Nomura Securities has said it could not confirm media reports saying that the corporate client was a real estate firm run by a relative of a former racketeer. It has also said that the suspected dealings were made on the judgement of the two former directors and not by Nomura itself.
The Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper quoted sources close to the watchdog as saying that the two executives conducted the illicit deals in the belief that they were part of company business.

The Yomiuri said Nomura's in-house investigation discovered the firm diverted a total of about 70 million yen in profits to Tokyo-based real estate firm between March 1993 and September 1996 in at least five separate installments.
The real estate firm is run by a younger brother of a former sokaiya racketeer, it said.
A Nomura spokesman said the company could not comment on its in-house findings as the case was under SESC investigation.

Sokaiya extort money from a company by threatening to disturb shareholders' meetings, or by offering to prevent a disruption of the proceedings. Japanese commercial law has prohibited paying off racketeers since 1982.

A government source told Reuters on Tuesday that the SESC had been investigating Nomura since last September and the probe was now centred on whether and how Nomura provided profits to a corporate customer. The investigation was likely to take at least a few more weeks, he said.

Under the Securities and Exchange Law, the SESC could advise the finance minister to hand down administrative punishment if it finds evidence of breaches of the securities exchange act. The heaviest penalty would be the revocation of Nomura's brokerage licence and suspension of its business for up to six months.
Under the law, the SESC could also pass the case to prosecutors to pursue criminal action.
